theory_title: Which one actually costs you less
theory_content: The new regime has lower slab rates and almost no deductions; the old regime has higher rates and allows 80C, 80D, HRA and home loan interest. The crossover depends entirely on how many deductions you genuinely claim. Someone paying rent, repaying a home loan and maxing 80C is often better off under the old regime; someone with few deductions is almost always better off under the new one. Compute both; do not assume.

Sell listed equity or an equity fund within twelve months and the gain is short-term, taxed at 20%. Hold beyond twelve months and it is long-term, taxed at 12.5% above an annual exemption of ₹1,25,000. The difference between selling at eleven months and thirteen is a third of the tax on the gain, for doing nothing.

theory_title: Using a loss you already have
theory_content: Realised capital losses offset realised capital gains in the same year, and unused losses carry forward for eight years if you file on time. Selling a losing position and rebuying a similar one resets your cost basis and banks the loss. India has no wash-sale rule, but the carry-forward requires the return to be filed by the due date.

The ₹1,25,000 annual LTCG exemption does not carry forward. Selling enough long-held units each year to realise a gain just under it, then rebuying, raises your cost basis at zero tax cost. Over a long holding period this measurably reduces the eventual bill for a few minutes of work each March.
